https://ai-online.com/2026/08/joker-juni.text: John Larkin 2 weeks ago 2 min read Pickering Group has announced that Daniel Hubáček, a recent graduate of the local Třinec high school, has won the competition to build a PickBot robot, aimed at students and held as part of the Invent Arena technology, science and innovation fair in the Czech Republic. Pickering Group has a large manufacturing business in the Třinec region, employing more than 400 people in the production of Pickering Electronics’ reed relays, Pickering Interfaces’ modular systems for signal switching and simulation and software for use in electronics testing, and cable and connector solutions for its connectivity division, Pickering Connect. The three group companies collaborated to create the ‘Build Your Own PickBot’ competition to raise the company’s profile, particularly among students in technical fields. Comments Anna Říhová, Pickering Czech Republic’s Communications and HR Marketing Specialist: “We wanted students to experience the creativity and problem solving involved in engineering, while introducing them to the career opportunities available locally. We engaged with students primarily through social media for six months, culminating in the contest at Invent Arena.” Each student team received an electronics kit from Pickering which, over the course of a month, they used to assemble, program and eventually guide their remote-controlled robot around an obstacle course on the show floor. During development, students were encouraged to chat with Pickering’s engineers for advice. Entries were evaluated over several categories including creativity, custom software, aesthetic design and speed on the track. It wasn’t just the students who were excited about Pickering’s PickBot competition; other visitors to the event were also able to try out Pickering’s track with their own robots. Younger visitors from elementary schools were also able to try driving Pickering’s models on the track. The winner, Daniel Hubáček with his entry, Joker Junior, received – appropriately enough – a 3D printer. About Pickering Group The privately-owned Pickering Group comprises three electronics manufacturers: reed relay company, Pickering Electronics; Pickering Interfaces, designers and manufacturers of modular signal switching & simulation products; and Pickering Connect, which designs and manufactures cables & connectors. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP US news Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists Associated Press Sun 27 Sep 2026 18.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms. Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph). Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument , a national conservation area, early this week. Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands. “Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center. Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east. View image in fullscreen Members of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP Near Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation. Residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala , which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island. About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family. Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact. “We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said. Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support. Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo. The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes. View image in fullscreen Yellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters Meanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds. Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph). Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, or SMN , said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday. Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas. The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane. One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion. “Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.” Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival. Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect. Photograph: Lee Jin-man/AP Stock markets Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets Business news – live updates Larry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is coming Kalyeena Makortoff Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.38 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 04.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points. Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%. The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry Elliott Read more Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI. The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July. The sell-off came after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September , marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month. “Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said. Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.” The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit. The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits. European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%. In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.
